title: Tocqueville Among the Homeschoolers
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio adapts a commencement address to homeschool graduates to resolve a tension in his own thinking: he is both a long-time school choice advocate and an avowed institutionalist. He argues that the standard choice case, built on consumers, markets and competition, explains why families leave schools but not what they do next. Through Tocqueville's habit of association, he reframes homeschooling families as producers who build co-ops, ensembles and leagues rather than merely exiting. From this he draws a larger claim that the highest purpose of educational freedom is to form citizens who accept responsibility for building and renewing institutions. He insists this does not diminish public schools and that stewardship may mean leaving or staying. The closing charge is for choice advocates themselves to explain what freedom is for, not just why families leave.
points: Choice advocacy has leaned on economic arguments and the failures of public schools, which casts choice as an escape hatch and under-sells it.
Homeschooling families who found co-ops, teachers and activities are doing the Tocquevillian work of institution-building, not simply opting out.
Pondiscio proposes a progression from liberty and markets to pluralism to institution-building as the deepest justification for educational freedom.
Stewardship is the shared lesson: citizens either create, sustain or repair institutions, and sometimes that means staying to renew them.
The line America has plenty of consumers and needs builders is the speech's practical charge to graduates and to choice advocates.
quotes: I’ve spent much of my career arguing for educational choice. At the same time, I consider myself an unabashed institutionalist. Healthy institutions—from schools and churches to libraries and Little League—form the indispensable infrastructure of society.

That last line surprised even me as I wrote it. Because it occurred to me that the most diligent homeschooling families are performing a profoundly American act of strengthening civil society. Tocqueville famously observed that Americans possessed a remarkable habit of association. Faced with problems, they didn’t simply petition the state. They gathered their neighbors, formed organizations, accepted responsibility, and built institutions together.
Seen in this light, homeschooling is not simply an act of exit. It’s an act of institution-building. Parents organize co-ops, recruit teachers, and share curricula.

Too often, we make the case for choice simply by cataloging the failures of public schools. We point to bureaucracy, ideology, declining achievement, parental frustration, or the inability of large systems to meet every child’s needs. Those concerns are real; I’ve made some of those arguments myself. But they cast school choice primarily as an escape hatch. And while that’s a valid argument, it’s also an impoverished one.

The purpose of educational freedom is not simply to help families find better schools. Nor is it only to create competition, or even to maximize parental choice. Its highest purpose is to cultivate citizens who are willing to accept responsibility for building institutions worthy of a free society.

We’ve become very good at explaining why families leave schools. We should spend an equal amount of time explaining what educational freedom is ultimately for. Its purpose is not only to expand choice. It is to form citizens who are prepared to inherit, build, sustain, and renew the institutions upon which a free society ultimately depends.
